title: The amoraim
hook: the sages of the Gemara, who discussed the Mishnah for three centuries

segments.voice: Yesterday, the tanna, and your line: the teachers of the mishnah. Rabbi Meir, who lit up the sages' eyes. Did you say someone's name along with what they taught you? Day one thousand sixty-six.

A sage is bathing in the Jordan River. A rough stranger sees him from the bank and, in one leap, jumps into the water after him. The sage is Rabbi Yochanan. The stranger is a man the Talmud calls Resh Lakish, and the story says he had been living as a robber. Rabbi Yochanan looks at him and says: your strength should be for Torah. Resh Lakish answers: your beauty should be for women. They strike a deal. If Resh Lakish will turn to study, Rabbi Yochanan will give him his sister in marriage. He does. And the robber becomes a sage whose words fill the Talmud. Today's word is what he became.
screen: `A LEAP INTO THE JORDAN.` → `YOUR STRENGTH FOR TORAH.` → `THE ROBBER BECOMES A SAGE.`

segments.voice: Amora. In the plural, amoraim. Yesterday's tannaim gave the Mishnah its words. The amoraim are the sages who came after, in the land of Israel and in Babylonia, and spent generations discussing those words line by line. Their discussion is the Gemara. Put the Mishnah and the Gemara together and you have the Talmud. The word amora is Aramaic, and Jastrow's dictionary of Talmudic Aramaic ties it to the verb to say: a speaker, an expounder. A few pairs to know: Rav and Shmuel in Babylonia. Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish in the land of Israel. Later, Abaye and Rava. Notice they are remembered in pairs. For them, explaining was something done with someone. Back to the riverbank story, which the Talmud tells in tractate Bava Metzia. Years later, after a bitter quarrel, Resh Lakish dies, and Rabbi Yochanan is crushed. The sages send him a brilliant student, Rabbi Elazar ben Pedat, to study with him. Every time Rabbi Yochanan says something, Rabbi Elazar answers: there's a teaching that supports you. And Rabbi Yochanan can't bear it. In paraphrase, he says: are you like the son of Lakish? When I said something, he would raise twenty-four objections, and I'd give twenty-four answers, and the matter would become clear on its own. You only tell me I'm right. I know I'm right. The story ends in grief, with Rabbi Yochanan crying out for his friend. For the amoraim, explaining wasn't agreeing. It was pushing back, hard, until the teaching came clear.
screen: `AFTER THE TANNAIM, THE AMORAIM.` · `AMORA: ONE WHO SAYS, WHO EXPOUNDS.` · `RAV AND SHMUEL; ABAYE AND RAVA.` · `TWENTY-FOUR OBJECTIONS, AND IT CAME CLEAR.` · then, large: `THE EXPLAINERS.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: learn one amora's name. Take Resh Lakish, the man who leapt into the river. Sit, and breathe, and say his name quietly a few times until it stays. Then let the rest of the bell go to a question. Who in your life pushes back on you, in a way that leaves you clearer instead of smaller? A friend, a sibling, a colleague who asks the second question. Hold their face in your mind for a while. If you pray, you can give thanks for them. If not, just notice what they've given you. The bell holds the time.
Amora. One of the sages of the Gemara, who discussed the Mishnah line by line, tied in the dictionary to the verb to say. Today's word.
Your line: the explainers. Today, when someone agrees with you too quickly, ask them for one objection. Day one thousand sixty-six.

howItsDone: Talmud study is traditionally done in pairs, a chavruta, where two learners read aloud, question each other and argue their way to the meaning of a passage.

pairs: kept saying, a teaching supports you

myth: the tannaim gave the Mishnah its words. the amoraim discussed it, line by line, in the Gemara.

fork.setup: you're Rabbi Yochanan. your partner in study has died. the sages send you a brilliant student who supports every word you say. what do you do?
options: welcome the support and go on teaching.
tell him you need objections, not agreement.
fork.reveal: he asks, are you like the son of Lakish? he raised twenty-four objections, and the answers made the matter clear. the story ends in his grief.

original.note: Aramaic: a sage of the Gemara; plural amoraim, אָמוֹרָאִים.

trapdoor: what you thought: the amoraim were the next generation of rabbis, nothing more.
what it means: the sages after the Mishnah, in the land of Israel and Babylonia, who explained it line by line in the Gemara.
what a scholar hears: a word tied to saying, and Bava Metzia 84a, where Rabbi Yochanan mourns a partner whose objections made the law come clear.
recall: the yearly anniversary of a death

sources.ref: Marcus Jastrow, A Dictionary of the Targumim, the Talmud Babli and Yerushalmi, and the Midrashic Literature (1903), s.v. amora

notes: Bava Metzia 84a paraphrased: Resh Lakish leaps into the Jordan after Rabbi Yochanan; 'your strength for Torah' / 'your beauty for women'; Yochanan offers his sister; Resh Lakish's death after a quarrel; Rabbi Elazar ben Pedat's 'there is a baraita that supports you'; 'twenty-four objections ... twenty-four answers'; Yochanan's grief. The number twenty-four is the text's own. 'Had been living as a robber' renders the Talmud's description of him as a bandit (some readers say a gladiator). Please confirm.

The quarrel (over when knives and weapons become susceptible to impurity) is mentioned only as 'a bitter quarrel'; the story's darker ending (Yochanan losing his mind with grief, the sages praying for his death) is softened to 'the story ends in grief'. Please confirm this is acceptable.
Amora tied to 'say, expound' via Jastrow (cited). The amora was also the speaker who relayed a teacher's lecture aloud; not mentioned. Please confirm.
Pairs named (Rav and Shmuel; Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish; Abaye and Rava) without dates. The outline's 'three centuries' is not stated, under the claims rule.
Editor: removed the superlative 'the standard dictionary' and named Jastrow, the cited source.
